rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding comparison identifies al-Akhnas ibn Shariq as the person about whom the slanderer verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: ويل لكل همزة لمزة ، والمنزول فيه الأخنس بن شريق

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another view explains the plural because the Kaaba is the qibla of Muslim mosques and Jerusalem is the qibla of others.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: جمعت لأنها قبلة المساجد كلها، يعني الكعبة للمسلمين، وبيت المقدس لغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking to ruin mosques can mean literal demolition, as of Jerusalem, or figuratively disabling remembrance there and barring worshippers, which leads to ruin.
rows.anchor: إما حقيقة، كتخريب بيت المقدس، أو مجازا بانقطاع الذكر فيها ومنع قاصديها منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse calls preventing remembrance ruin and treats sustained remembrance and prayer as building the mosques; both are figurative usages.
rows.anchor: فجعل المنع خرابا، كما جعل التعاهد بالذكر والصلاة عمارة، وذلك مجاز

rows.speaker: المروزي
rows.claim: Al-Marwazi says the question teaches that corrupt belief causes mosque destruction, while sound belief causes their flourishing.
rows.anchor: وقال المروزي: قال ومن أظلم ليعلم أن قبح الاعتقاد يورث تخريب المساجد

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declarative wording predicts what will occur, a Qur'anic report of the unseen and glad tidings that Islam will prevail over its enemies.
rows.anchor: هذه جملة خبرية قالوا تدل على ما يقع في المستقبل، وذلك من معجز القرآن، إذ هو من الإخبار بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāʾifīna is accusative as a circumstantial accusative; the exception is an unrestricted exception from circumstances.
rows.anchor: إلا خائفين: نصب على الحال، وهو استثناء مفرغ من الأحوال

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads illā khīfan, a broken plural of khāʾif; its form reflects that he did not treat it as a verse-end rhyme, with wāw changed to yāʾ as in ṣawm/ṣaym.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: إلا خيفا، وهو جمع خائف، كنائم ونوم، ولم يجعلها فاصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported explanation makes their fear the humiliation, subjection, and jizya that would be imposed on them.
rows.anchor: هو ما يلحقهم من الصغار والذل والجزية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported explanation is fear that believers will attack them.
rows.anchor: أو من أن يبطش بهم المؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation locates the fear in the course of litigation, which itself entails fear.
rows.anchor: أو في المحاكمة، وهي تتضمن الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Christians enter Jerusalem fearing a painful beating.
rows.anchor: أو ضربا موجعا، لأن النصارى لا يدخلون بيت المقدس إلا خائفين من الضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers that they should enter God's mosques fearing God and dreading His punishment; a house appointed for worship should be honored, maintained, and entered reverently.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المعنى: أولئك ما ينبغي لهم أن يدخلوا مساجد الله إلا وهم خائفون من الله وجلون من عقابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates the blame by analogy: one who meets a friend of God ought to honor him, so killing him is a gross reversal of the proper response.
rows.anchor: ما كان له أن يلقاه إلا معظما له مكرما أي هذه حالة من يلقى وليا لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offenders deserve great blame because they did the opposite of the reverence and honor that mosques should receive.
rows.anchor: ففي ذلك تقبيح عظيم على ما وقع منه، إذ كان ينبغي أن يقع ضده

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future-event interpretation misses the force of mā kāna lahum, which denies that entering this way was proper or sought; a plain prediction would say mā yadkhulūnahā.
rows.anchor: لكان اللفظ: أولئك ما يدخلونها إلا خائفين، ولم يأت بلفظ: ما كان لهم

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes the phrase as God's decree in the Preserved Tablet to support believers until unbelievers enter mosques only in fear.
rows.anchor: ما كان لهم في حكم الله، يعني أن الله قد حكم وكتب في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some infer that unbelievers may enter mosques if afraid; Abū Ḥayyān rejects that inference in light of his preferred reading of the verse.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الناس: وفيها دلالة على جواز دخول الكفار المساجد على صفة الخوف

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view treats the declarative form as a command to Muslims to make unbelievers afraid, prompted by predictions of later entry and destruction of the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: لفظه لفظ الخبر، ومعناه الأمر لنا بأن نخيفهم

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says that the Ethiopian ذو السويقتين will demolish the Kaaba stone by stone; it was cited to argue against reading the verse as a future prediction.
rows.anchor: أن ذا السويقتين من الحبشة يهدم الكعبة حجرا حجرا

words: مَا كَانَ لَهُمْ أَن يَدْخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān finds the imperative reading and its appeal to later events far-fetched; his interpretation removes the alleged contradiction and defeats these alternatives.
rows.anchor: ودلالتها على الأمر لنا بالإخافة لهم بعيدة جدا، وإذا حملنا الآية على ما ذكرناه

words: فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة ليسوؤا وجوهكم وليدخلوا المسجد
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about the coming of the latter promise is not an allusion to the Day of Resurrection; he defers fuller discussion to its place.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة، فليس ذلك كناية عن يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awlāʾika follows the semantic sense of man in the opening, not its grammatical form; matching form or meaning is possible for relative, conditional, and interrogative man.
rows.anchor: أولئك، حمل على معنى من في قوله: ومن أظلم، ولا يختص الحمل فيها على اللفظ وعلى المعنى

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some take the verse as proof that unbelievers may not enter a mosque; Abū Ḥayyān says the entry question belongs to jurisprudence and the verse, on his reading, does not prove it.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الناس في قوله تعالى: ومن أظلم: الآية، دليل على منع دخول الكافر المسجد

words: لَهُمْ فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا خِزْىٌۭ وَلَهُمْ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The penalties mirror the offenses: worldly abasement answers silencing remembrance, while the fire's bodily destruction answers their attempt to ruin mosques; 4:56 describes renewed skin after burning.
rows.anchor: وأما العذاب العظيم في الآخرة، فهو العذاب بالنار، وهو إتلاف لهياكلهم وصورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly disgrace needs no qualifier because its legal forms are equivalent whether a belligerent is killed or captured or a protected person pays jizya.
rows.anchor: لم يحتج إلى وصف. ولما كان العذاب متفاوتا، أعني عذاب الكافر وعذاب المؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife punishment is called great to distinguish an unbeliever's torment from a believer's, since their punishments differ.
rows.anchor: ولما كان العذاب متفاوتا، أعني عذاب الكافر وعذاب المؤمن، وصف عذاب الكافر بالعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported gloss identifies worldly disgrace with Islamic conquests, naming Constantinople, Amorium, and Rome.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخزي هو الفتح الإسلامي، كالقسطنطينية وعمورية ورومية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the worldly disgrace as the jizya imposed on protected non-Muslims.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جزية الذمي، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss identifies the disgrace as their expulsion from the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طردهم عن المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: المروزي
rows.claim: Al-Marwazi says the disgrace will be the Mahdi's killing of them when he appears.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قتل المهدي إياهم إذا خرج، قاله المروزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reported gloss takes the disgrace as exclusion from mosques.
rows.anchor: وقيل: منعهم من المساجد

rows.speaker: بعض معاصرينا
rows.claim: A contemporary says every unbelieving group suffers worldly humiliation: Jews and Christians through killings, expulsions, conquests, jizya, and imposed marks or terms; Arab polytheists through defeat, idol-breaking, expulsion from Arabia, and death unless they convert.
rows.anchor: قال بعض معاصرينا: إن على كل طائفة من الكفار في الدنيا خزيا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the disgrace is promised for the end of the world, when Muslims will conquer the Romans, a conquest not yet realized.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: معناه في آخر الدنيا، وهو ما وعد الله به المسلمين من فتح الروم

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī allegorizes ruined sanctuaries as hearts, souls, spirits, and inner secrets ruined by desire and attachment; disgrace is the veil and torment comes from settling for spiritual ranks.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري: في قوله تعالى: ومن أظلم الآية، إشارة إلى ظلم من خرب أوطان المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls this allegory strange and says Qur'anic wording does not support it, as with most interpretations of this group.
rows.anchor: وهذا تفسير عجيب ينبو عنه لفظ القرآن، وكذا أكثر ما يقوله هؤلاء القوم

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators take the dual east and west as verbal nouns for the sun's rising and setting; Abū Ḥayyān says the following clause about turning does not favor this.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض المفسرين إلى أنهما اسما مصدر، والمعنى أن لله تولي إشراق الشمس من مشرقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular can refer to a region or a source located in a region; the plural reflects daily changing horizons, and the dual the winter and summer rise and set points.
rows.anchor: وأفرد المشرق والمغرب باعتبار الناحية، أو باعتبار المصدر الواقع في الناحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawallaw may mean turning one's face toward a direction, or turning one's back; on the latter reading, wherever one turns away and faces elsewhere, God's face is there.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التولية: الاستقبال بالوجوه. وقيل: معناها الاستدبار من قولك: وليت عن فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view addresses mosque-destroyers: wherever they turn in flight, God observes them; al-Ḥasan's third-person reading fits the pronouns of the surrounding verses.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليست في الصلاة، بل هو خطاب للذين يخربون المساجد، أي أينما تولوا هاربين عني

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads fa-ayn amā yuwallū, in the third person; this aligns with the surrounding third-person references to their disgrace and their claim about God's son.
rows.anchor: ويقويه قراءة الحسن: فأينما تولوا، جعله للغائب، فجرى على قوله: لهم في الدنيا خزي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī construes turning as facing the qibla, supported by commands to face the Sacred Mosque; Abū Ḥayyān calls this a good specification of the otherwise unrestricted wording.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ففي أي مكان فعلتم التولية، يعني تولية وجوهكم شطر القبلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators sometimes place jurisprudential disputes here: prayer toward a mistaken qibla after inquiry in darkness, obligatory or voluntary prayer on an animal, and absentee funeral prayer if the verse concerns Najāshī; Abū Ḥayyān says these belong to fiqh.
rows.anchor: من صلى في ظلمة مجتهدا إلى جهة، ثم تبين أنه صلى لغير القبلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-thamma wajhu Allāh is the answer to the conditional clause and is an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: فثم وجه الله، هذا جواب الشرط، وهي جملة ابتدائية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Muqātil take God's face here as the qibla or direction He commanded people to face, the direction in which His pleasure lies.
rows.anchor: الحسن ومجاهد وقتادة ومقاتل. وقيل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation treats wajh as an additional expression, so the meaning is that God, with His knowledge and judgment, is there.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الوجه هنا صلة، والمعنى فثم الله أي علمه وحكمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil take face as a reference to God's essence, as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس ومقاتل: أو عبر عن الذات بالوجه، كقوله تعالى: ويبقى وجه ربك

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ understands the phrase as work done for God and cites a poetic line where al-wajh is paired with work.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى العمل لله، قاله الفراء، قال: أستغفر الله ذنبا لست محصيه

rows.speaker: أبو منصور
rows.claim: Abū Manṣūr says face can mean rank or honor, yielding God's majesty and greatness as the sense.
rows.anchor: قاله أبو منصور في المقنع. وحيث جاء الوجه مضافا إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some affirm a distinct revealed attribute called God's face, beyond what reason establishes about the Necessary Being.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب بعض الناس إلى أن تلك صفة ثابتة لله بالسمع، زائدة على ما توجبه العقول

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya and others reject affirming an attribute from an ambiguous word whose meaning is unknown and unintelligible in Arabic; Abū Ḥayyān prefers established Arabic senses and rejects bodily interpretation.
rows.anchor: وضعف أبو العالية وغيره هذا القول، لأن فيه الجزم بإثبات صفة لله تعالى بلفظ محتمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a divine expression can suggest corporeality, he reads it through a sound Arabic sense: a valid shared literal meaning or, otherwise, metaphor; metaphor is abundant in Arabic.
rows.anchor: إذا كان للفظ دلالة على التجسيم فنحمله، إما على ما يسوغ فيه من الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes those who place God in a location or direction: permitting all directions shows no direction is His locus, while every direction belongs to His dominion.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: فأينما تولوا فثم وجه الله رد على من يقول: إنه في حيز وجهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because claiming God has a child is an extreme and impossible error, the verse begins with glorification to disavow it before rebutting the claim.
rows.anchor: أتى باللفظ الذي يقتضي التنزيه والبراءة من الأشياء التي لا تجوز على الله تعالى

words: بَل لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything in the heavens and earth, including those alleged to be God's children, belongs to Him; parenthood conflicts with ownership because a father does not own his child.
rows.anchor: أي جميع ذلك مملوك له، ومن جملتهم من ادعوا أنه ولد الله. والولادة تنافي الملكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators insert the jurisprudential question of a person buying a parent, child, or other close relative, but Abū Ḥayyān says it belongs to fiqh.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر بعض المفسرين هنا مسألة من اشترى والده أو ولده أو أحدا من ذوي رحمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creatures are submissive and obedient to God; as a slave obeys an owner, their obedience confirms His ownership, and their nature differs from a parent's offspring.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر أن الكل مملوك لله تعالى، ذكر أنهم كلهم قانتون له، أي مطيعون خاضعون له

rows.speaker: غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unattributed theologian says God has eternally commanded nonexistents conditionally upon their existence, with eternal power and knowledge despite created effects and events occurring later.
rows.anchor: والمعتقد في هذه الآية أن الله لم يزل آمرا للمعدومات بشرط وجودها

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī glosses qaḍā as completing, perfecting, and finishing a matter; fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu means He says on its account.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: وإذا قضى أمرا، أي أتقنه وأحكمه وفرغ منه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says God addresses the thing with Be while it is nonexistent because, being known to Him, it is as though already existent.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قال له كن، وهو معدوم، لأنه بمنزلة الموجود، إذ هو عنده معلوم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the command neither precedes nor follows existence: the thing exists through the command as it is commanded; resurrection likewise coincides with God's call, as 30:25 states.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: أمره للشيء بكن لا يتقدم الوجود ولا يتأخر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in lahu may refer to the matter, the decree implied by qaḍā, or the intended thing implied by the context.
rows.anchor: فالهاء في له تعود على الأمر، أو على القضاء الذي دل عليه قضى

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī says God knows what will be and what is; Be addresses what exists in His knowledge to bring it into our visible world.
rows.anchor: وقال مكي: معنى الآية أنه عالم بما سيكون وما هو كائن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes kāna as intransitive: Be means arise, and it arises; this is figurative representation, not literal speech, for creation enters existence immediately and without resistance.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كن فيكون، من كان التامة، أي احدث فيحدث، وهذا مجاز من الكلام وتمثيل ولا قول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the image of immediate obedience underscores that God's power is unlike bodily reproduction and thereby makes the claim of divine offspring untenable.
rows.anchor: أكد بهذا استبعاد الولادة، لأن من كان بهذه الصفة من القدرة

rows.speaker: السجاوندي
rows.claim: Al-Sajāwandī calls Be an analogy for the irresistible execution of God's command and cites a poem asking how a nonexistent could be addressed.
rows.anchor: قال السجاوندي: كن على التمثيل لنفاذ الأمر، قال: فقالت له العينان سمعا وطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed readings make Be a sign to angels that something has occurred, a way of conceiving what God knows will exist, or a command for an existing thing to change state.
rows.anchor: أو علامة للملائكة بحدوث الموجود، أو على تقدير ما تصور كونه في علمه

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī argues that if Be were created, it would need another created Be, without end; this regress is impossible and supports uncreated divine speech.
rows.anchor: قال المهدوي: وفي هذه الآية دليل على أن كلام الله غير مخلوق

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī rejects a figurative reading absent evidence, arguing that the emphatic verbal noun in the verse and in God's speaking to Moses establish literal speech.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يحمل على المجاز، إذ ذلك إنما يكون في الجمادات

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī also transmits the interpretation that fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn means that it comes to be.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن معنى فإنما يقول له كن فيكون بكونه

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: The Muntakhab rejects a literal sequence in which God says Be and only then the thing exists, offering four interpretations; it favors the first, immediate efficacy of God's creative power without deliberation.
rows.anchor: وفيه وجوه: الأول: وهو الأقوى، أن المراد نفاذ سرعة قدرة الله في تكوين الأشياء

rows.speaker: أبو الهذيل
rows.claim: Abū al-Hudhayl's alternative makes the utterance a sign that angels understand as notice that God has brought something into being.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنها علامة يعقلها الملائكة، إذا سمعوها علموا أنه أحدث أمرا، قاله أبو الهذيل

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm's alternative addresses already existing people whom God turns into apes, as in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: ومن جرى مجراهم، وهو قول الأصم

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: A further, weaker alternative treats Be as an order to living people to die and to the dead to live.
rows.anchor: الرابع: أنه أمر للأحياء بالموت، وللموتى بالحياة، والكل ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the apparent wording suggests a command when God wills to create, but reason rules out addressing nonexistents or making God a locus of temporal events; Be is figurative representation of instantaneous, unobstructed creation.
rows.anchor: لكن دليل العقل صد عن اعتقاد مخاطبة المعدوم، وصد عن أن يكون الله تعالى محلا للحوادث

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read fa-yakūnu in the nominative, either as a new sentence meaning 'then it is' (attributed to Sībawayh) or coordinated with yaqūlu, which al-Ṭabarī selects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فيكون بالرفع، ووجه على أنه على الاستئناف، أي فهو يكون

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects on semantic grounds to coordinating fa-yakūnu with yaqūlu; the excerpt ends before completing his reason.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهو خطأ من جهة المعنى، لأنه يقتضي أن القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies those who do not know as the Jews who lived in the Prophet's time.
rows.anchor: اليهود الذين كانوا في عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رافع بن خزيمة
rows.claim: Rāfiʿ ibn Khuzayma, a Jew, demanded that God speak to them so they could hear Him; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قال رافع بن خزيمة، من اليهود: إن كنت رسولا من عند الله، فقل لله يكلمنا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies those who do not know as the Meccan polytheists.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: مشركو مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view includes all these groups because all made such demands; which predecessors are meant depends on whether the referent is Arab unbelievers or Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإشارة بقوله: الذين لا يعلمون إلى جميع هذه الطوائف، لأنهم كلهم قالوا هذه المقالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs lack knowledge because they had neither scripture nor a prophetic tradition; Jews or Christians lack it because they fail to follow and act on what they know.
rows.anchor: فنفي عنهم العلم، لأنهم لم يكن لهم كتاب، ولا هم أتباع نبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of 'know' is omitted for brevity: the point is to deny that knowledge characterizes them, not to deny knowledge of a particular subject.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول العلم هنا اقتصارا، لأن المقصود إنما هو نفي نسبة العلم إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their challenge asks why God does not speak as He spoke to angels or Moses, or send a sign; it expresses arrogance and obstinacy and disdains the signs already given.
rows.anchor: ومعمول القول، الجملة التحضيضية وهي: لولا يكلمنا الله كما يكلم الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative 'or a sign comes to us' means they demanded one of two things—speech or a sign—while rejecting the signs they had already received.
rows.anchor: أي هلا يكون أحد هذين، إما التكلم، وإما إتيان آية؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the present speakers are Arab or Meccan unbelievers, their predecessors are earlier rejecting nations; if Jews or Christians, they are their ancestors.
rows.anchor: فالذين من قبلهم هم الأمم المكذبة من أسلافهم وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mithla qawlihim is an appositive to the syntactic position of the kāf; similarity need not be identical wording, only the same kind of improper demand.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب مثل قولهم على البدل من موضع الكاف. ولا تدل المثلية على التماثل في نفس المقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to both the present challengers and their predecessors: just as their sayings match, their hearts match in blindness and ignorance, as in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: الضمير عائد على الذين لا يعلمون، والذين من قبلهم. لما ذكر تماثل المقالات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported interpretation says their hearts are alike in unbelief.
rows.anchor: قيل: تشابهت قلوبهم في الكفر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the clause in the passive as a declarative statement; Ubayy's mā tasʾalu and Ibn Masʿūd's lan tusʾal are also declarative, with Ibn Masʿūd's necessarily independent.
rows.anchor: قراءة الجمهور: بضم التاء واللام. وقرأ أبي: وما تسأل. وقرأ ابن مسعود: ولن تسأل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority and Ubayy readings may be an independent sentence, which is likelier, or circumstantial; Ibn Masʿūd's reading must be independent.
rows.anchor: فالقراءة الأولى، وقراءة أبي يحتمل أن تكون الجملة مستأنفة، وهو الأظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an independent statement, it means the Prophet is not responsible for why unbelievers failed to believe; he must only convey, which comforts him and teaches that no one bears another's sin.
rows.anchor: أنك لا تسأل عن الكفار ما لهم لم يؤمنوا، لأن ذلك ليس إليك، إن عليك إلا البلاغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read as a circumstantial clause, it qualifies the Prophet's sending: he is not answerable for the unbelievers' failure to believe.
rows.anchor: وأما الحال فعطف على ما قبلها من الحال، أي وغير مسؤول عن الكفار

rows.speaker: نافع ويعقوب
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read with an open tāʾ and jussive lām, making the phrase an apparent prohibition against asking about the unbelievers' fate.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع ويعقوب: ولا تسأل، بفتح التاء وجزم اللام، وذلك على النهي

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī reports that the Prophet wondered what had become of his parents, and this verse was then revealed.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن كعب القرظي: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ليت شعري ما فعل أبواي» ، فنزلت

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: The Muntakhab considers that occasion implausible because the Prophet already knew their ultimate fate; ʿIyāḍ says they were revived for him and believed.
rows.anchor: واستبعد في المنتخب هذا، لأنه عالم بما آل إليه أمرهما. وقد ذكر عياض أنهما أحييا له فأسلما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says it is soundly reported that God permitted the Prophet to visit his parents.
rows.anchor: وقد صح أن الله أذن له في زيارتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also finds that occasion discordant with the context, which addresses Jews, Christians, and Arab polytheists who rejected the Prophet's mission; making the subject his parents requires an abrupt break in discourse.
rows.anchor: لأن سياق الكلام يدل على أن ذلك عائد على اليهود والنصارى ومشركي العرب، الذين جحدوا نبوته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the prohibition is not literal but intensifies the horror of their punishment, like saying 'do not ask about him' when someone is in a terrible state.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يحتمل أن لا يكون نهيا حقيقة، بل جاء ذلك على سبيل تعظيم ما وقع فيه أهل الكفر من العذاب
